title: Offshore Wind Turbine Foundations
analyses: Coupled wind, wave and current loading analysis
Fatigue and remaining useful life analysis
Monopile lateral and axial capacity analysis
Foundation overturning, sliding and bearing capacity analysis
Accidental impact and structural damage analysis
scope: Applicable to monopiles, jackets, tripods, gravity-based foundations, suction buckets and other offshore wind foundations.

models.text: The suite should implement force and moment equilibrium, Euler–Bernoulli beam theory, Timoshenko beam theory, elastic foundation beam formulations, Euler buckling, plate and shell equations, structural modal equations, geometric stiffness analysis, pile axial resistance relationships and nonlinear lateral soil resistance formulations.

The suite should include blade element momentum theory, blade element aerodynamic models, actuator-disc theory, actuator-line theory, Prandtl tip-loss and hub-loss corrections, Glauert corrections, dynamic inflow models, dynamic stall models such as Beddoes–Leishman, blade pitch control models, aerodynamic thrust and torque models, IEC-based turbulence representations, Kaimal turbulence spectra, Mann spectral turbulence modelling and extreme wind gust models.

The foundation loading system should employ Morison's equation, Airy wave theory, Stokes higher-order theory, stream-function wave theory, wave diffraction and radiation methods where applicable, JONSWAP wave spectra, current drag models and nonlinear wave-current interaction. For complex geometries and highly nonlinear loading, the suite may additionally employ potential-flow boundary-element analysis and Navier–Stokes CFD.

The suite should include API-style lateral pile resistance formulations where applicable, axial pile resistance methods, nonlinear pile–soil springs, elastic continuum models, Mohr–Coulomb soil plasticity, Modified Cam-Clay, cyclic p–y degradation, strain accumulation models, monopile-specific soil reaction models, suction bucket bearing models, uplift resistance models, Terzaghi and Meyerhof bearing-capacity formulations, consolidation theory, cyclic soil liquefaction models and seabed scour correlations.

The suite should implement coupled aero-hydro-servo-elastic equations of motion, modal analysis, Campbell diagrams, modal damping models, Rayleigh damping, wind-wave joint probability modelling, rainflow cycle counting, Palmgren–Miner damage accumulation, S–N relationships, spectral fatigue analysis, resonance screening and nonlinear time-history analysis.

Pile-driving simulation should incorporate one-dimensional stress-wave propagation, Smith's wave-equation pile-driving method, soil resistance to driving models and hammer–pile–soil interaction. Suction-bucket installation should employ seepage, penetration resistance, effective stress and soil–structure interaction models. Hybrid frameworks should integrate turbine aerodynamic loads, controller dynamics, foundation flexibility, nonlinear soil reactions, fatigue damage and stochastic environmental simulation. IEC 61400-3-1 provides a design framework for fixed offshore wind turbines, including design-load cases and environmental loading considerations.

inputs.text: Monopile diameter, penetration depth, wall thickness, taper geometry, jacket member dimensions, tripod geometry, suction-bucket diameter, skirt length and foundation arrangement.
Rated power, rotor diameter, hub height, nacelle mass, rotor mass, blade masses, turbine operating speeds and assembly centre of gravity.
Tower sectional dimensions, steel grades, flange geometry, transition piece dimensions, grout details and connection stiffness.
Rotor thrust, aerodynamic torque, blade loads, operational wind speed distribution, turbulence intensity, wind shear and directional wind statistics.
Water depth, water-level variation, wave height, period and direction, wave spectra, current profiles and extreme environmental conditions.
Borehole records, CPT cone resistance, sleeve friction, soil layering, undrained shear strength, relative density, friction angle and soil stiffness.
Axial load-transfer curves, lateral resistance relationships, soil degradation parameters, cyclic soil properties and foundation boundary stiffness.
Steel elastic and strength properties, grout properties, concrete compressive strength, fatigue classifications and corrosion allowances.
Pile driving hammer energy, blow efficiency, pile penetration records, suction pressure, installation tolerances and temporary support conditions.
Seabed grain-size distribution, bed shear stress, erosion characteristics, scour depth estimates and scour protection properties.
Wind-wave joint probability distributions, operational cycles, load histories, S–N curves and joint stress concentration factors.
Earthquake ground motion, liquefaction susceptibility, cyclic soil resistance and ground deformation.
Turbine operational states, shutdown conditions, emergency stops, design load cases and required service life.

Structural reliability, design compliance and remaining useful life
subtitle: Monopiles, jackets, tripods, suction buckets, gravity foundations and integrated turbine–foundation interaction.
ic: The initial conditions shall establish the installed or installation-stage geometry of the monopile, jacket, tripod, gravity-based foundation or suction-bucket foundation. These shall include the foundation penetration depth, seabed elevation, pile orientation, transition-piece arrangement, tower connection and foundation material condition.

The initial geotechnical conditions shall specify soil layering, in-situ effective stresses, pore-water pressure, soil density, undrained shear strength, soil stiffness and the condition of disturbed or remoulded soil where installation effects are relevant. Initial pile stresses, installation-induced residual stresses and soil consolidation conditions shall be included where significant.

For operational analysis, the turbine and foundation shall begin from a defined equilibrium condition under structural weight, buoyancy, rotor thrust, tower loading and the selected environmental conditions. Rotor speed, blade pitch, nacelle orientation and turbine control states shall be initialized when a coupled turbine simulation is performed.

The initial conditions for fatigue and vibration analysis shall identify the existing damage state, tower-foundation stiffness and vibration equilibrium. Seabed scour analysis shall begin from a specified initial seabed profile, with or without existing scour protection. Seismic analysis shall use an established foundation equilibrium and appropriate initial soil stress conditions.
bc: The foundation shall interact with the seabed through appropriate axial, lateral, rotational and contact restraints. Monopiles may use nonlinear pile–soil springs or continuum soil models, while gravity foundations shall use distributed contact, bearing and frictional conditions. Suction buckets shall require skirt–soil interaction and, where applicable, internal and external pore-pressure conditions.

At the turbine interface, the boundary conditions shall transfer tower-base forces, moments, rotor-induced dynamic loading and control-dependent reactions into the foundation. Fully coupled simulations shall preserve displacement and rotational compatibility between the tower and foundation.

Environmental boundaries shall prescribe wind inflow, turbulence, wave motion, current velocity profiles, water level and extreme storm conditions. Seabed scour simulations shall use sediment and flow boundary conditions consistent with the selected hydrodynamic and sediment-transport model.

During pile installation, the pile head shall receive specified hammer forces, penetration loading or imposed driving motion. Suction-foundation installation shall prescribe pump-induced pressure differences and foundation penetration constraints. Seismic boundaries shall impose appropriate ground-motion histories, while structural fatigue boundaries shall represent cyclic wind-wave loading over the operating environment.

calibration: Foundation models should be calibrated using offshore geotechnical investigations, cone penetration tests, laboratory soil tests, instrumented pile tests and operational wind turbine monitoring.

Pile–soil interaction parameters should be adjusted using measured monopile lateral displacements, rotations, bending strain distributions, foundation stiffness and cyclic load behaviour. Soil stiffness degradation, cyclic accumulation and load-transfer behaviour should reflect the specific soil type and installation conditions.

Integrated aero-hydro-servo-elastic models should use turbine supervisory control and data acquisition records, measured rotor thrust where available, tower accelerations, measured natural frequencies, nacelle movements and structural strain measurements.

Hydrodynamic coefficients should be calibrated against controlled wave-current experiments and field measurements. Structural damping should be calibrated using shutdown tests, operational modal analysis and measured vibration decay.
Scour prediction parameters should be calibrated using laboratory sediment experiments, measured seabed grain distributions and repeated bathymetric surveys.
Pile driving and suction-bucket penetration models should be calibrated using installation records, penetration resistance, measured hammer response, suction pressure and foundation movement.
Fatigue damage models should use representative weld fatigue tests, foundation strain histories and documented material behaviour.
verification: Structural and foundation calculations should be verified through analytical member benchmarks, pile response benchmarks, frame analysis checks and soil–foundation load-transfer tests.
Monopile and jacket finite-element models should undergo mesh refinement and sensitivity studies involving pile dimensions, embedment, soil stiffness and structural connection conditions.

Coupled turbine-foundation simulations should be verified through component-level tests and integrated benchmark comparisons. Rotor, tower, foundation, controller and soil models should be tested individually before full coupling.
Dynamic verification should check natural frequencies, mode shapes, damping implementation and consistency of structural response under prescribed loading.
Time-step convergence should be demonstrated for transient wind, wave, current and turbine control events.
Pile driving and suction foundation models should undergo penetration-step sensitivity tests, contact convergence checks and force-balance assessments.
Buckling, overturning, sliding and bearing calculations should be checked against established analytical or benchmark numerical solutions.
Scour and seabed erosion calculations should undergo spatial and temporal convergence studies, sediment transport conservation checks and sensitivity assessments.
validation: Natural frequencies, tower accelerations, foundation rotations and mudline bending response should be compared against independent operational turbine measurements.
Monopile lateral and axial capacity predictions should be validated using full-scale or appropriately scaled instrumented pile tests.
Cyclic pile response should be compared with experimental evidence covering representative soil conditions, load amplitudes and loading histories.
Integrated structural response should be validated against field-measured turbine loads and dynamic behaviour over different operating wind speeds and sea states.
Scour predictions should be tested against repeated seabed surveys or independent laboratory scour experiments.
Pile driving and suction installation predictions should be assessed using recorded penetration, hammer performance, suction pressure and installation response.
Fatigue predictions should be compared with independently observed structural damage, inspection findings or representative fatigue tests.
Validation should explicitly identify the foundation types, soil conditions, turbine configurations and environmental conditions covered by the evidence.

geometry.text: Monopiles, transition pieces, jacket foundations, tripods, gravity-based foundations, suction buckets, anchor foundations, towers and foundation–soil interaction domains.

geometry.cat: Conventional and universal CAD geometry formats
geometry.text: STEP, IGES, Parasolid, ACIS, IFC, DXF and supported DWG should handle pile geometries, transition pieces, structural nodes, flanges, stiffeners, grout interfaces, foundation shells, concrete bases and suction-bucket skirts.

SDNF, IFC structural and infrastructure models, beam-centreline models, pile-section tables, stratigraphic geometry in GML or structured XML/JSON and coordinate-based foundation layout files should be supported. Such datasets are particularly appropriate when foundation analysis requires both structure and ground geometry.

Abaqus INP, Nastran BDF, ANSYS CDB, Gmsh MSH, MED, UNV, VTK/VTU, CGNS (.cgns) and Exodus can be used for compatible foundation, contact, soil continuum and coupled structural discretizations. Imported soils and structural elements must retain region boundaries and material-assignment information where available.

GeoTIFF (.tif, .tiff), ESRI ASCII Grid (.asc), XYZ bathymetric points, LAS/LAZ, E57, PLY, OBJ, STL, LandXML (.xml) and HDF5 (.h5, .hdf5) with documented data schemas should be supported for seabed profiles, soil-interface geometry, scanned foundations and installation-site reconstruction.
